nameStory: The Northern Cinnabar Polypore gets its striking name from cinnabar, the brilliant red-orange mineral that was prized by ancient civilizations for making vermillion pigment. When you spot this fungus glowing like a sunset against dark bark, you'll immediately understand why early naturalists thought of that precious mineral. The bright orange-red color is so distinctive that it practically announces itself in the forest!
description: This eye-catching bracket fungus looks like nature's own bright orange shelf sprouting from dead wood. The Northern Cinnabar Polypore forms vibrant orange to red-orange semicircular brackets that can grow up to about 5 inches across and about half an inch thick. Unlike many drab brown bracket fungi, this species is impossible to miss with its brilliant coloration that stays vivid even as it ages. It's a saprophyte, meaning it feeds on dead wood and helps break down fallen logs and dead branches.

idTips.label: Cap Color
idTips.description: Brilliant orange to red-orange color that's unmistakable - like a traffic cone or bright autumn leaf. The color stays vibrant and doesn't fade much with age.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underneath, tiny round pores (not gills) that are cream to pale orange, with 2-4 tiny holes per millimeter. Run your finger across - it feels smooth to slightly rough.

idTips.label: Cap Texture
idTips.description: Surface feels smooth to slightly velvety when young, becoming harder and more leathery with age. No hair or fuzz like some brackets.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms shelf-like brackets directly from wood with no stem, often growing in overlapping clusters like orange roof shingles.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a white spore print if you place the cap pore-side down on dark paper overnight.

idTips.label: Safety Note
idTips.description: Inedible and tough - never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification, as some fungi can be toxic.

habitat: Look for this colorful bracket on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It's particularly common on dead oak, maple, and birch, where it helps decompose the wood. You'll often find it in both lowland woods and higher elevation forests, typically on wood that's been dead for a while but isn't completely rotten yet.

seasonality.spring: New bright orange brackets begin emerging on dead wood as temperatures warm. Fresh specimens have the most vivid coloration and smooth texture.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with many fresh, vibrant specimens appearing after rain. This is the best time to see the most brilliant orange colors.
seasonality.fall: Brackets continue growing and remain colorful, though older specimens may start showing signs of age. Still easily spotted among falling autumn leaves.
seasonality.winter: Old brackets persist on wood but become harder, darker, and less colorful. Still identifiable by shape and pore structure, though not as eye-catching.

funFact: This fungus actually produces its own natural antibiotic called cinnabarinic acid to protect itself from harmful bacteria - essentially making its own medicine to stay healthy while it decomposes wood!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other orange bracket fungi, but the Northern Cinnabar Polypore's brilliant, traffic-cone orange color is more vivid than most relatives. Turkey-tail can sometimes have orange zones but shows distinct color bands and is usually much more muted. Remember: if it's blazing orange and has tiny pores underneath, you've likely found your cinnabar polypore.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "Northern" Cinnabar Polypore, this species is actually found worldwide and isn't restricted to northern regions - the name mainly distinguishes it from its close relative, the Southern Cinnabar Polypore. The bright orange color comes from natural pigments that also help protect the fungus from UV damage and other environmental stresses.
compareHints: Within the Trametes genus, this species stands out for its solid, brilliant orange color without the multicolored bands typical of Turkey-tail or the white/cream colors of many other relatives. While Cinnabar Bracket (Trametes sanguinea) is very similar, the Northern Cinnabar Polypore tends to have a more consistently bright orange color and slightly different pore structure. The intense, uniform orange coloration makes it one of the most distinctive members of this otherwise variable genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Turkey-tail differs from its Trametes relatives by having the most variable and vibrant color patterns - while Northern Cinnabar Polypore is distinctly reddish-orange and Hairy Bracket is notably fuzzy, turkey-tail displays the widest range of colors in distinct concentric bands.
Among its Trametes relatives, Gilled Polypore is instantly distinguished by having true gills instead of the pores found in Turkey-tail or the maze-like patterns of White Maze Polypore.
Unlike the smooth, velvety turkey-tail with its colorful concentric zones, lumpy bracket is much plainer and bumpier.
Unlike its Trametes relatives like turkey-tail which form flat, colorfully zoned shelves, the little nest polypore is immediately recognizable by its unique cup shape.
Among its Trametes relatives, Hairy Bracket stands out for its distinctly fuzzy upper surface - most other species in this genus like Turkey-tail and Cinnabar Bracket have smooth, almost glossy caps.

Among the turkey-tail relatives, Trametes pubescens stands out for its uniform cream coloration and velvety texture, lacking the colorful zones of turkey-tail or the bright colors of cinnabar brackets.
